questions.q: What does a model extraction attack actually target?
options: The victim's training data storage bucket directly
The victim's source code repository
The victim's raw weights file on disk
The victim's public prediction API, using its input/output behavior to train a substitute model
questions.explain: Model extraction never touches the training pipeline, code, or weights — it reconstructs an approximation purely from input/output pairs collected through the model's prediction API.

questions.q: In the Tramer et al. (2016) "Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs" research, what did researchers demonstrate?
options: Production-style ML-as-a-service classifiers could be reconstructed to near-exact fidelity, sometimes recovering exact parameters, with a relatively small number of queries
Model extraction is only possible if the attacker already has the training data
Confidence scores and hard labels leak exactly the same amount of information
Extraction requires physical access to the server hosting the model
questions.explain: The paper showed several production-style classifiers could be extracted to high fidelity, in some cases exactly, with low thousands of queries — all through the public API, no insider access required.

questions.q: Why does returning a full confidence vector (e.g. "cat: 0.87, dog: 0.11, other: 0.02") increase extraction risk compared to returning only the top label?
options: It doesn't increase risk — labels and confidence vectors leak identical information
Confidence vectors are only returned to admin users, so there's no risk
It reveals the model's distance from the decision boundary, giving a substitute model gradient-like signal that speeds convergence
Confidence vectors take longer to transmit, which slows the attacker down
questions.explain: A hard label gives one bit of boundary information per query; a confidence vector reveals how far a point sits from that boundary, which is exactly the signal an attacker's substitute model needs to converge quickly.

questions.q: Why is model extraction a genuine business risk rather than just an academic curiosity?
options: It only affects models that are already open source
It can gut a per-query pricing model, hand a competitor the product's actual differentiator, and feed adversarial-example crafting offline against the stolen copy
It has no real-world cost because models can always be retrained for free
It is prevented automatically by HTTPS encryption on the API
questions.explain: Extraction undermines per-query pricing, hands competitors the behavior that differentiates the product, and gives attackers a private copy to craft adversarial examples against with no rate limits or logging.

questions.q: How does model extraction connect to adversarial examples, covered later in Chapter 5?
options: A substitute model built from extraction lets an attacker craft adversarial inputs offline against their own copy, which frequently transfer back to attack the real model
Adversarial examples require the original model's weights, so extraction is unrelated
Extraction and adversarial examples are two names for the exact same attack
Adversarial examples can only be crafted against models that have already been extracted and then re-trained from scratch
questions.explain: Once an attacker has a substitute model approximating the decision boundary, they can generate adversarial examples against it with no query limits or logging, and those often transfer back to the real, original model.
